mainTopic: How a group shares costs and rescued property, and a robber's liability when thugs seize a stolen field
overview: The amud opens at the end of a challenge. A worker sent with food to a sick person is paid even if the sick person died or recovered, so a rescuer who failed should also be paid. רבי answers that the worker finished his job and the rescuer did not. Next come ברייתות about groups sharing costs. A ransom paid to bandits is split by money, a guide's wages may also be split per person, and cargo thrown off a sinking ship is shared by weight. Donkey drivers and sailors may agree to replace each other's losses, but not losses caused by carelessness. Another ברייתא says a traveler who saves a caravan's goods from bandits saves them for everyone, unless he announced he was saving them for himself. רמי בר חמא, רבא and רב אשי each explain why his words matter. Then a new משנה teaches that a robber whose stolen field is seized by thugs owes nothing in a regional disaster, but must replace it if the loss came because of him. The גמרא explains the wording of the משנה and tells of a man who showed the ריש גלותא's wheat to thugs and was made to pay by רב נחמן. רב יוסף's question about why it matters whether that payment was law or a fine continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The worker sent with food for a sick person still gets full pay
steps.stepSummary: The challenger finishes his proof. A worker hired to bring cabbage and plums to a sick person gets his full wage even if the sick person already died or got better.
steps.simpleTranslation: [If someone hired a worker] to bring cabbage and plums to a sick person, and the worker went and found that the sick person had died or recovered, he still gives him his full wage!
steps.whatsHappening: We are joining the end of a challenge. The challenger quotes a case where a worker is paid in full even though his work turned out to be useless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier discussion was about a person who tried to rescue his friend's donkey and had made a deal to be paid for it. The challenger argues that pay depends on effort, not on results, because the food-carrier is paid even though the sick person no longer needed the food. So the rescuer should be paid even if he did not manage to save the donkey.

keyTerms.meaning: A kind of plum (literally, Damascus fruit)

steps.confusionAlert: This text begins in the middle of a sentence. The words 'someone who hires a worker' come just before it. The point of the case is that the food was not needed in the end, and the worker is still paid.

phrases.english: to bring cabbage and plums to a sick person,
and he went and found that he had died or recovered –
he gives him his wage in full!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a challenge that began before this text, about a rescuer who made a deal to be paid and then failed to save the donkey.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that a rescuer who failed to save the animal gets nothing, even though he made a deal to be paid
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A hired worker is paid for his effort even when the result turns out useless, so the failed rescuer should also be paid.

steps.title: The cases are different because the worker finished his job
steps.stepSummary: רבי answers that the cases are not alike. The food-carrier did what he was sent to do, but the rescuer did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Are these comparable?! There, the agent did his assignment. Here, the agent did not do his assignment.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי pushes back the challenge by showing the two cases are not alike.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worker was hired to bring the food, and he did bring it. Nobody needing it is not his fault. The rescuer was hired to save the donkey, and he did not save it, so he never finished the job he was hired for. Pay depends on finishing the assigned task, not on whether that task turned out to be useful.

keyTerms.meaning: Are they comparable? (a way of rejecting a comparison)
Agent, the one sent to do a job
His assignment, the job he was sent to do

steps.whatToRemember: A worker gets paid when he finishes the job he was hired for, even if it turns out useless. If he never finished the job, he does not get paid.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the line for paying workers: pay depends on doing the assigned task, not on how things turn out in the end.

phrases.english: He said to him: Are they comparable?!
There, the agent performed his assignment,
here, the agent did not perform his assignment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 1 by showing the two cases are different.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing the two cases are different
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Pay is earned by effort alone, so the failed rescuer should be paid.
steps.terutzMaskana: Pay is earned by finishing the assigned task. The food-carrier finished his; the rescuer did not.

steps.title: A ransom paid to bandits is split by how much money each person has
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that when bandits threaten a caravan, the ransom is split according to each traveler's money, not equally per person.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: A caravan was traveling in the desert, and a troop of bandits rose up against it to rob it. They calculate the payment according to money, and they do not calculate it according to people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new topic with a ברייתא about how travelers in a caravan share a ransom paid to bandits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The bandits want to take property, so the ransom protects each traveler's money. Someone carrying more money is protected more, so he pays a bigger share. The cost is not split equally per person.

keyTerms.meaning: A troop of bandits or soldiers
People (literally, souls); here, a per-person split

phrases.aramaic: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: שְׁיָירָא שֶׁהָיְתָה מְהַלֶּכֶת בַּמִּדְבָּר,
phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: A caravan that was traveling in the desert,
and a troop rose up against it to rob it –
they calculate according to money,
and they do not calculate according to souls.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: שְׁיָירָא שֶׁהָיְתָה מְהַלֶּכֶת בַּמִּדְבָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: how travelers share costs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A ransom paid to bandits is split according to how much money each traveler carries, not per person.

steps.title: A hired guide may be paid per person, following local custom
steps.stepSummary: If the caravan hired a guide to lead the way, his wages may also be split per person. In any case, travelers should not depart from the usual custom of donkey drivers.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if they hired a guide who walks ahead of them, they calculate even according to people. And they should not change from the custom of the donkey drivers.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with a different case, a hired guide, where a per-person split is also allowed. It ends by saying the accepted custom decides.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A guide protects the travelers' lives and not just their money. Everyone's life is worth the same, so splitting his wages per person also makes sense. The last line adds that whatever split the donkey drivers usually use should be kept.

keyTerms.meaning: A guide or scout who leads the way
Even according to people, so a per-person split is also used
The custom of the donkey drivers
They should not change or depart from

steps.whatToRemember: Ransom to bandits is split by how much money each person has. A guide's wages may also be split per person. In all cases, keep the accepted custom of the travelers.
steps.confusionAlert: The word 'אַף' (even) means the per-person split is added, not that it replaces the split by money.

phrases.english: And if they hired a scout who goes before them –
they calculate even according to souls;
and they should not depart from the custom of the donkey drivers.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with a different case: a hired guide instead of a ransom.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A hired guide's wages may also be split per person, and the travelers' usual custom should be followed.

steps.title: Donkey drivers may agree to replace a lost donkey
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: חמרים may agree in advance to replace any member's lost donkey, but not if he lost it through negligence. If he asks for money so he can help guard, they do not listen to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Donkey drivers are allowed to make a deal: if anyone loses his donkey, the group will get him another one. If he lost it through carelessness, they don't replace it. If it wasn't his fault, they do. If he says, 'Give me the money instead, and I'll keep helping guard,' they don't have to listen to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with the donkey drivers from the last step and teaches that they may make a group insurance deal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The group may set up a shared fund to replace lost donkeys. This deal only covers losses that were not the owner's fault. The owner also cannot demand cash instead of a donkey, because the group wants him to have a real donkey of his own to protect.

keyTerms.meaning: To make a condition or agreement

phrases.english: The donkey drivers are permitted to stipulate
that anyone whose donkey becomes lost
we will provide him with another donkey.
If it was lost through negligence, they do not provide one;
phrases.notes: בכוסיא means through his own carelessness, when the loss was his fault.

phrases.english: if not through negligence, they provide him one.
And if he said: "Give me, and I will guard,"
phrases.notes: He means: give me money instead of a donkey, and I'll still help guard the caravan.

phrases.english: they do not listen to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא about traveling caravans, adding a rule about replacing lost donkeys.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: חמרים may agree to replace a donkey lost without negligence. They need not replace one lost through negligence, and need not give cash instead of a donkey.

steps.title: Isn't the last rule obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא needs to teach that they do not give him money. This seems obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the last rule of the ברייתא, that they don't give money to the man who wants to guard. This sets up the next step's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who has no donkey left has no reason to guard the caravan carefully, so of course the group won't pay him cash. The גמרא wants to know what new point the ברייתא is teaching.

phrases.english: It is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions why the final clause of the ברייתא in step 5 needed to be said.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What new point does the ruling 'they do not listen to him' teach, if it seems obvious?

steps.title: The rule applies even when he still has another donkey
steps.stepSummary: The rule is needed for a driver who still owns a second donkey. You might think he will guard well anyway. The ברייתא teaches that guarding one donkey is not like guarding two.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a case where he still has another donkey. You might have said: he is guarding anyway for the sake of his other donkey. So the ברייתא teaches us that guarding one donkey is not the same as guarding two.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question by explaining the case where the rule is really needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he still has a donkey, he has his own reason to guard, so we might think cash is enough. The ברייתא says no. A man with two donkeys to protect guards much more carefully than a man with one, so the group may insist on giving him a real donkey.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for this case

steps.whatToRemember: The group may give a real replacement donkey instead of cash, because having more of your own property in the caravan makes you guard more carefully.

phrases.aramaic: לָא צְרִיכָא, דְּאִית לֵיהּ חֲמָרָא אַחֲרִינָא.
phrases.english: No, it is needed where he has another donkey.

phrases.aramaic: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא: הָא קָא מְינַטַּר לֵיהּ;
phrases.english: You might have said: he is guarding it anyway;
phrases.notes: He'll be guarding for the sake of the donkey he still has, so cash might seem fine.

phrases.english: so it teaches us

phrases.aramaic: שָׁאנֵי נְטִירוּתָא דְחַד מִנְּטִירוּתָא דְבֵי תְרֵי.
phrases.english: that guarding one is different from guarding two.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דְּאִית לֵיהּ חֲמָרָא אַחֲרִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא question by limiting the ruling to a case where he still has another donkey.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ruling applies even when he owns another donkey, because a man guarding two donkeys is more careful than a man guarding one.

steps.title: Cargo thrown off a ship in a storm is shared by weight
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא: when a ship in a storm must lighten its load, the loss is divided by weight, not by money value. The usual custom of sailors is kept.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: a ship was sailing at sea, and a big wave rose up to sink it. They lightened its load. They figure each person's share by weight, not by money value. And they should not change from the usual custom of sailors.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about sharing a loss in a group, this time on a ship.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the bandit case (step 3), the ransom was split by money. Here the loss is split by weight, since the danger comes from the heavy load. Local sailors' custom still decides how things are done.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with the bandit case. There the payment was by money value; here, with cargo thrown overboard, it is by weight.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A ship that was traveling at sea;
a gale rose against it to sink it,
and they lightened its load,
they calculate according to weight,
and they do not calculate according to money;
and they should not change from the custom of sailors.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: סְפִינָה שֶׁהָיְתָה מְהַלֶּכֶת בַּיָּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new ברייתא about dividing group losses, parallel to the caravan case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Cargo thrown overboard to save a ship is shared by weight, not by value, and sailors' custom is followed.

steps.title: Sailors may agree to replace a lost ship
steps.stepSummary: Like the חמרים, sailors may agree to replace a member's lost ship, but not if it was lost through negligence or sailed somewhere ships do not go.
steps.simpleTranslation: Sailors are allowed to make a deal: if anyone loses his ship, the group will get him another one. If he lost it through carelessness, they don't replace it. If it wasn't his fault, they do. And if he sailed off to a place where ships don't go, they don't replace it.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives the same insurance rule for sailors that we learned for donkey drivers, with one extra limit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The group deal covers only honest, unavoidable losses. Sailing into waters where ships don't normally go counts as taking a risk on yourself, so the group does not have to pay for it.

keyTerms.meaning: Set out or sailed off (away from the normal route)

steps.whatToRemember: Group insurance deals, for donkeys or ships, cover only losses that were not the owner's fault and that happened on the normal route.

phrases.english: And the sailors are permitted to stipulate
that anyone whose ship was lost
we will provide him with another ship.
If it was lost through negligence, they do not provide one;
if not through negligence, they provide him one.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי פֵּירַשׁ לְמָקוֹם שֶׁאֵין הַסְּפִינוֹת הוֹלְכִין –
phrases.english: And if he sailed off to a place where ships do not go,
they do not provide one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ship ברייתא with a replacement rule parallel to the donkey drivers' rule in step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sailors may agree to replace a lost ship, but not one lost through negligence or one that sailed to a place where ships do not go.

steps.title: Isn't the sailing rule obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא needs to say that a sailor who goes where ships do not go counts as negligent.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't this obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the last part of the sailors' ברייתא from Step 9. Of course sailing where ships never go is negligent, so why say it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Anyone who takes a ship somewhere dangerous is clearly careless. So the extra line in the ברייתא looks unneeded. This sets up the next step, which shows a case where it is not so obvious.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious. The גמרא asks why something needed to be said at all.

phrases.english: It is obvious!
phrases.notes: He means the line from the ברייתא: a ship that sailed to a place where ships do not go.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the need for the last clause of the ברייתא in Step 9.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why does the ברייתא need to say that sailing to a place ships do not go is negligence?

steps.title: The safe distance changes by season
steps.stepSummary: In ניסן ships keep one rope-length from shore and in תשרי two. A sailor who uses the תשרי route during ניסן is negligent, even though it is a normal route at another time of year.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for this case. In ניסן ships stay one rope-length away, and in תשרי they stay two rope-lengths away. This sailor sailed in ניסן to the place used in תשרי. You might have thought he is just taking his usual route. So the ברייתא teaches us that he is still negligent.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the rule is needed for a route that is safe in one season but not in the season he sailed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A beginner might think a route that sailors really use cannot be called 'a place ships do not go.' The ברייתא teaches that safety depends on the season. Using the תשרי route during ניסן is negligence, so the other sailors do not have to replace his ship.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not needed for the simple case. It is needed for this special case.
A rope, used here as a measure of distance from shore.
You might have said. This introduces the mistaken first thought.
It teaches us. This introduces the real lesson.

phrases.english: No, it is needed
for in Nisan they distance one rope-length,
phrases.notes: He means ships keep this distance from the shore.

phrases.english: and in Tishrei they distance two rope-lengths,

phrases.aramaic: וְקָא אָזֵיל בְּיוֹמֵי נִיסָן לִמְקוֹם תִּשְׁרֵי;
phrases.english: and he went during the days of Nisan to the place of Tishrei;
you might say: he is taking his usual path and going,
so it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 10 by giving a case where the rule is not obvious.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The rule covers a sailor who used a route proper for one season during a different season. That still counts as negligence.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since it is a real sailors' route, he is just following the normal path and is not negligent.
steps.terutzMaskana: A route that is right for תשרי is negligent in ניסן.

steps.title: Rescuing a caravan from bandits
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא: if bandits rob a caravan and one member saves the goods, he saves them for everyone. If he announced he is saving them for himself, they become his.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: A caravan was traveling in the desert. A band of raiders attacked and robbed it. One of the travelers got up and rescued the goods. He rescued them for everyone. But if he said, 'I am rescuing for myself,' he rescued them for himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about who owns goods that one traveler rescues from bandits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא has two parts. In the first part, a rescuer who says nothing returns the goods to all the owners. In the second part, saying 'for myself' makes him the owner. The next step will ask how both parts can be true together.

keyTerms.meaning: A caravan, a group traveling together.
A band of raiders or soldiers.
For the middle, meaning for everyone together.

phrases.aramaic: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: שְׁיָירָא שֶׁהָיְתָה מְהַלֶּכֶת בַּמִּדְבָּר
phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: A caravan that was traveling in the desert
and a band of raiders arose and plundered it,
and one of them arose and rescued it,
he rescued it for everyone.
And if he said: 'I will rescue for myself,'
he rescued it for himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: שְׁיָירָא שֶׁהָיְתָה מְהַלֶּכֶת בַּמִּדְבָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: rescuing a group's property instead of sharing a group's losses.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If he says nothing, the rescued goods go back to everyone. If he says 'for myself,' they are his.

steps.title: How can both halves of the ruling be true?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the case is. If the owners could save their goods, even 'for myself' should not make them his. If they could not, even the silent rescuer should keep them.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If the owners are able to rescue, then even in the second part the goods should go to everyone. And if they are not able to rescue, then even in the first part the goods should be his.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא from Step 12. Its two parts seem to contradict each other in any case you choose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ownership should depend on whether the owners still had hope of getting their goods back, not on what the rescuer said. If they could save their goods, they never gave up, so the goods stay theirs. If they could not, they gave up, so anyone who saves the goods keeps them, even without saying so.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the exact circumstances?
The first part of a teaching.
The last part of a teaching.

steps.confusionAlert: 'Able to rescue' here means the owners themselves could have saved their goods. That is why they would not have given up hope on them.

phrases.english: What is the case?
If they are able to rescue,
then even in the latter part it should also be for everyone!
And if they are not able to rescue,
then even in the first part it should also be for himself!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the ברייתא from Step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The difference between the first and second parts of the caravan ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Ownership should depend on whether the owners could save their goods. Under either possibility, both parts of the ruling should come out the same.

steps.title: The caravan members were partners
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא says the caravan members owned the goods as partners. In a case like this, one partner may split off his share without the others agreeing. So saying 'for myself' counts as splitting, and staying silent does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא said: Here we are dealing with partners. In a case like this, a partner may divide the property without his partner's agreement. If he said 'for myself,' he has divided. If he did not say it, he has not divided.
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר חמא answers the question from Step 13. The case is about partners, so the rescuer's words really do change the result.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling is not about whether the owners gave up hope. The goods were owned jointly, and in this kind of emergency one partner may split the property on his own. Saying 'for myself' is his act of splitting, so what he rescues counts as his share. Without that statement, the partnership stays, and what he rescues belongs to everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: We are dealing with. This introduces a specific case.

steps.whatToRemember: The rescuer's statement matters because the caravan members were partners. Saying 'for myself' is how a partner splits off his share. Staying silent keeps the property shared.

phrases.english: Rami bar Hama said:
Here we are dealing with partners,

phrases.aramaic: וּכְגוֹן זֶה – שׁוּתָּף חוֹלֵק שֶׁלֹּא לְדַעַת חֲבֵירוֹ;
phrases.english: and in a case like this, a partner may divide without his fellow's consent;
if he said it, he has divided,
if he did not say it, he has not divided.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא: הָכָא בְּשׁוּתָּפִין עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 13 by placing the ברייתא in a case of partners.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the ברייתא to a specific case (partners), so the rescuer's statement decides the result.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Ownership depends only on whether the owners could rescue their goods, so the rescuer's words should not matter.
steps.terutzMaskana: Among partners, saying 'for myself' splits off his share, so his words decide the outcome.
steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches that in a case like this, one partner may split jointly owned property on his own, and that a spoken statement can be what makes the split happen.

steps.title: רבא: The rescuer was a hired worker
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers differently: the ברייתא is about hired workers, and it follows רב, who says a worker may quit even in the middle of the day.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Here we are dealing with hired workers, and it follows רב, for רב said: A worker may back out even in the middle of the day.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a new answer to the קשיא from Step 13. He says the rescuer was a worker hired by the caravan, and he quotes a rule from רב that he will use.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רמי בר חמא explained the case with partners. רבא explains it with a hired worker instead. Because a worker may quit at any time, saying 'for myself' can mean he quit before he rescued the goods.

keyTerms.meaning: To back out of a commitment
In the middle of the day (in the middle of the job)

phrases.english: Rava said:
Here we are dealing with hired workers,
and it follows Rav, for Rav said:
A worker may back out
even in the middle of the day.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to the קשיא in Step 13, replacing רמי בר חמא's partnership explanation.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case: the rescuer is a hired worker, not a partner.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The rescuer was an ordinary member of the caravan, so it seemed strange that his words would change who owns the goods.
steps.terutzMaskana: He is a worker who may quit at any time. His words decide whether he rescued as a worker or as a free person.

steps.title: Why a worker's rescue belongs to his employer until he quits
steps.stepSummary: While a worker has not quit, he is treated like part of the employer's domain, so what he saves goes to the employer. He may quit because Jews are servants of ה׳, not servants of servants.
steps.simpleTranslation: As long as he has not backed out, he is considered to be in the employer's domain. And when he does back out, that is for a different reason, as it is written: 'For to Me the children of Israel are servants,' and not servants to servants.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how רבא's answer works. While the worker stays on the job, anything he saves belongs to his employers. Once he quits, he is free and can keep what he saves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A silent rescuer is still working, so the goods go to everyone in the caravan. One who says 'for myself' has quit, so he rescues as a free person and keeps goods the owners could not save. His right to quit comes from a פסוק: a Jew may not be locked in as a servant to another person.

keyTerms.meaning: In the domain (authority) of the employer

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבא, a worker who has not quit is 'owned' by his employer for the work time, so what he saves goes to the employer. Quitting, which the תורה allows at any time, frees him to rescue for himself.

phrases.english: As long as he has not backed out,
he is considered to be in the employer's domain,
and when he backs out,
it is for a different reason,
as it is written: 'For to Me the children of Israel are servants,'
and not servants to servants.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how רבא's worker case fits both halves of the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the mechanism: before quitting he belongs to the employer, and after quitting he is free.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without explanation, it is unclear why a worker's words would matter.
steps.terutzMaskana: Silence means he is still working, so the goods go to everyone. Saying 'for myself' means he quit, so the goods are his.

steps.title: רב אשי: The owners could save the goods only with difficulty
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says the case is where the owners could have saved the goods, but only with great difficulty. If the rescuer announced his intent, he keeps the goods. If not, they belong to everyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: This is where they could save it only with difficulty. If he revealed his intention, it is for himself. If he did not reveal his intention, it is for everyone.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a third answer to the קשיא from Step 13. He picks a middle case, between 'they could save it' and 'they could not save it.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The קשיא assumed only two options. רב אשי adds a third: saving it was possible but very hard. In that case the owners have not fully given up hope, so the rescuer's words decide. If he says 'for myself' and they stay quiet, they have given up. If he says nothing, nothing has changed and the goods are still everyone's.

keyTerms.meaning: For the middle, for everyone together

steps.whatToRemember: There are now three answers to the caravan ברייתא: רמי בר חמא (partners splitting off a share), רבא (a hired worker who quits), and רב אשי (saving the goods was possible but hard).

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
This is where they could save it only with difficulty.
If he revealed his intention, it is for himself;
if he did not reveal his intention, it is for everyone.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: כְּשֶׁיָּכוֹל לְהַצִּיל עַל יְדֵי הַדְּחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third answer to the קשיא in Step 13, alongside רמי בר חמא and רבא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Finds a middle case that the קשיא's two options did not cover.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The owners either could save the goods or could not, so the rescuer's words should not matter.
steps.terutzMaskana: When saving was possible but hard, the owners' hope is uncertain, so the rescuer's announcement and their silence decide the outcome.

steps.title: New משנה: A stolen field seized by thugs
steps.stepSummary: If someone robs a field and thugs then take it from him: if it was a disaster across the whole region, the robber may tell the owner 'here is yours.' If the thugs took it because of the robber, he must give the owner another field.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One who robs a field from another, and thugs then took it: if it is a regional disaster, he says to him, 'Here is yours before you.' If it was because of the robber, he must provide him with another field.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with a new case. It asks whether a robber must pay when a field he stole is taken from him by violent thugs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A field cannot be carried off, so the question is who carries the loss when it is seized. If thugs grabbed all the land in the area, the owner would have lost it anyway, so the robber owes nothing. If the thugs took this field because of the robber, he caused the loss and must replace it.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה (marks the start of a new משנה)
A regional disaster, a blow to the whole area
To provide him with a different field

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the robber is always free just because land cannot really be stolen and moved. If the thugs took the field because of him, he must give the owner another field.

phrases.english: Mishnah:
One who robs a field from another
and thugs then took it,
if it is a regional disaster,
he says to him: 'Here is yours before you';
if it was because of the robber,
he must provide him with another field.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הַגּוֹזֵל שָׂדֶה מֵחֲבֵירוֹ וּנְטָלוּהָ מַסִּיקִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the caravan discussion and opens a new משנה about a stolen field.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a regional disaster the robber returns the field as it is, even though thugs hold it. If the thugs took it because of him, he must give the owner a replacement field.

steps.title: Both spellings of the word for thugs are correct
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק says the word for thugs in the משנה can be read as מסיקין or as מציקין. Both readings are correct.
steps.simpleTranslation: GEMARA: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: Whoever reads the משנה as 'מסיקין' is not making a mistake, and whoever reads it as 'מציקין' is not making a mistake either.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its discussion of the משנה with a point about wording. There are two versions of the word for 'thugs', and רב נחמן בר יצחק says both are fine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing about the law changes here. The question is only which spelling belongs in the משנה. רב נחמן בר יצחק says both are good, and the next two steps give a פסוק to support each one.

keyTerms.meaning: Thugs who 'eat up' or take over other people's property (spelled with ס)
Oppressors, people who cause distress (spelled with צ)

phrases.aramaic: גְּמָ׳ אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק:
phrases.english: GEMARA: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:
Whoever teaches 'massikin' is not mistaken,
phrases.notes: This is the word our משנה uses for the thugs who took the field (Step 18).

phrases.english: and whoever teaches 'matzikin' is not mistaken.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק: מַאן דְּתָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא's discussion of the משנה from Step 18 by clarifying a word in it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The word for thugs may be read as either מסיקין or מציקין; both are correct.

steps.title: A source for the reading מציקין
steps.stepSummary: The reading מציקין is supported by the פסוק 'in the siege and in the distress (מצוק)'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whoever reads 'מציקין' is not mistaken, because it is written: 'In the siege and in the distress.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the reading מציקין with a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק uses the word מצוק, meaning distress or pressure. So מציקין means 'people who cause distress', which fits thugs who seize land.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is written (introduces a פסוק)

phrases.english: Whoever teaches 'matzikin' is not mistaken,
as it is written: 'In the siege and in the distress.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a פסוק to support the second reading mentioned in Step 19.

steps.title: A source for the reading מסיקין
steps.stepSummary: The reading מסיקין is supported by the Aramaic תרגום of 'the locust shall consume', which uses the word סקאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whoever reads 'מסיקין' is not mistaken either, because it is written: 'The locust shall consume', and in Aramaic we translate it as: 'The סקאה shall consume it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the other reading, מסיקין, using a פסוק and its Aramaic translation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תרגום calls the locust סקאה, a word from the same root as מסיקין. A locust swarms in and eats up everything, so מסיקין means people who take over and 'eat up' other people's property.

keyTerms.meaning: And we translate (in the Aramaic תרגום)
Locust (Aramaic), from the same root as מסיקין

steps.whatToRemember: Both spellings work. מציקין means 'those who oppress', and מסיקין means 'those who eat up property like locusts'. Either way, the word means thugs.

phrases.english: And whoever teaches 'massikin' is not mistaken,
as it is written: 'The locust shall consume,'
and we translate it: 'The sakka'ah (locust) shall take it over.'
phrases.notes: סקאה sounds just like מסיקין. That shared sound is the whole proof.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a פסוק for the first reading mentioned in Step 19, which completes the discussion of the wording.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The פסוק 'יירש הצלצל' (דברים 28:42) and its Aramaic תרגום 'יחסניניה סקאה'

steps.title: Why does the משנה need to say 'because of the robber'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case the משנה's line 'if because of the robber, he is liable' is talking about. If it means the thugs took only his land, we already know that from the first line about a regional disaster.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'If it was because of the robber, he is liable.' What is the case? If you say the thugs seized only his land and not all the lands in the area, you already learned that from the first line: 'If it is a disaster across the whole region, he is exempt.' That implies that if it is not, he is not exempt!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the second line of the משנה and challenges it. The line seems to add nothing new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first line exempts the robber only when the whole region was hit (מכת מדינה). That already tells us that if only this field was taken, he must pay. So if the second line just means 'only his field was taken', it repeats what we already know. The גמרא wants to find a case that makes the second line necessary.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the circumstances?
A disaster that hits the whole region
From the first clause (of the משנה)

phrases.english: 'If it was because of the robber, he is liable.'
What is the case?
If you say that they seized his land
and did not seize all the lands,
you already learned this from the first clause:
'If it is a regional disaster, etc.'
which means if it is not, then not!
phrases.notes: He means: if it is not a regional disaster, the robber is not exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the wording of the משנה to the meaning of its second clause.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's clause 'אם מחמת הגזלן חייב'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Redundancy: the first clause already implies that the robber is liable when only his field was taken, so the second clause seems unnecessary.

steps.title: The robber pointed out the field to the thugs
steps.stepSummary: The second clause is needed for a case where the person never actually took the field himself. He only pointed it out to the thugs, and he is still liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a case where he pointed it out to them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by giving the second clause its own special case. The robber showed the thugs the field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Because of the robber' does not just mean that his field alone was taken. It means a case where he never actually took the field at all, but only showed it to the thugs. The clause teaches something new: even without taking it himself, the loss is his doing, so he must give the owner another field.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for (this case)

steps.confusionAlert: 'Because of the robber' here does not mean the thugs were angry at him personally. It means he himself showed them the field.

phrases.english: No, it is needed where he actually pointed it out.
phrases.notes: 'He' is the robber, and he pointed the field out to the thugs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the redundancy challenge of Step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the clause to a specific case (אוקימתא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The second clause just means the thugs took only the robber's field, which the first clause already implies.
steps.terutzMaskana: The clause teaches about a case where the robber himself pointed out the field to the thugs.

steps.title: Another version: forced to show his land, he showed the stolen field too
steps.stepSummary: In another version, gentiles forced a person to show them his land, and he showed them another man's field along with his own fields.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another version: What case are we dealing with here? Where gentiles forced him and demanded that he show them his land, and he showed them that field along with his own.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of the same answer and describes the case in more detail.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the robber was under pressure. The gentiles forced him to show them his own land. But he also pointed out the stolen field together with his own. Since he chose to include it, the loss is because of him, so he is liable.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here?

steps.whatToRemember: The robber is exempt only if the field was lost in a disaster across the whole region. If he caused the loss, for example by pointing out the field to the thugs, he must give the owner another field.

phrases.english: Another version:
What case are we dealing with here?
For example, where gentiles forced him,
and told him to show them his land,
phrases.notes: Some versions say the word in round brackets, and some say the word in square brackets.

phrases.english: and he showed that one along with them.
phrases.notes: 'That one' is the stolen field, and 'them' is his own fields.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second version of the answer in Step 23, with more detail about the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the clause to a specific case (אוקימתא), in an alternate version
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The second clause just repeats the implication of the first clause.
steps.terutzMaskana: The case is where gentiles forced him to show his own land, and he showed them the stolen field along with it.

steps.title: A man pointed out the ריש גלותא's wheat and was made to pay
steps.stepSummary: A man showed the ריש גלותא's wheat piles to thugs, and רב נחמן ruled that he must pay for the loss.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a man who showed the wheat piles of the ריש גלותא's household to thugs. The case came to רב נחמן, and he made the man pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real court case that matches what it just explained about pointing out property to thugs. רב נחמן ruled that the man who pointed out the wheat must pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man did not take the wheat himself. He only showed it to people who then grabbed it. Even so, רב נחמן made him pay, just like the robber in our משנה who pointed out the field.

keyTerms.meaning: the Exilarch, the leader of the Jews in בבל

phrases.english: There was a certain man who showed
piles of wheat
phrases.notes: The גמרא leaves it out, but he showed them to thugs, who then took the wheat.

phrases.english: belonging to the Exilarch's household.
The case came before Rav Nachman,
and Rav Nachman obligated him to pay.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a real-life case that fits the explanation that the robber pointed out the field to thugs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who points out another person's property to thugs, who then take it, must pay for it.

steps.title: Was the payment basic law or a fine?
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בר חייא, sitting in front of רב נחמן with רב יוסף behind him, asks if the ruling was דינא or קנסא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף sat behind רב הונא בר חייא, and רב הונא בר חייא sat in front of רב נחמן. רב הונא בר חייא asked רב נחמן: Did you make him pay because that is the law, or as a fine?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא first tells us who was sitting where, then רב הונא בר חייא asks רב נחמן a question about his ruling. He wants to know the reason behind the payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דינא means the man truly owes the money by basic Torah law. קנסא means the רבנן added a penalty to stop people from doing this, even though basic law would not require payment. The question is not whether he pays, but why.

keyTerms.meaning: a fine or penalty set by the רבנן

steps.confusionAlert: רב הונא בר חייא is not disagreeing that the man must pay. He only asks what kind of obligation it is.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef was sitting behind
Rav Huna bar Chiyya,
and Rav Huna bar Chiyya was sitting
in front of Rav Nachman.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב הוּנָא בַּר חִיָּיא לְרַב נַחְמָן:
phrases.english: Rav Huna bar Chiyya said to Rav Nachman:
Is it the law, or a fine?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב הוּנָא בַּר חִיָּיא לְרַב נַחְמָן דִּינָא אוֹ קְנָסָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the basis of רב נחמן's ruling in the story.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the payment was required by basic law (דינא) or as a rabbinic penalty (קנסא).

steps.title: רב נחמן: it comes straight from our משנה
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן answers that it is basic law, taught in our משנה about the robber who must give a field, which was explained as a case of pointing it out.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: It is our משנה, as we learned: If it is because of the robber, he must give him a field. And we explained that this is where he pointed out the field.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן answers that the payment is basic law, and he proves it from our משנה. He uses the explanation the גמרא gave earlier, that the robber pointed out the field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the משנה itself says the robber must pay, this is דינא, not just a fine. The man with the wheat did the same thing as the robber: he pointed out property to thugs. So the same law applies to him.

keyTerms.meaning: to provide him with a field

steps.whatToRemember: רב נחמן holds that one who points out property to thugs owes payment by basic law, learned from our משנה about the robber.

phrases.english: He said to him: It is our Mishnah,
as we learned:
If it is because of the robber,
he is obligated to provide him with a field;
and we established it as where he pointed it out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב הונא בר חייא's question by pointing to the משנה.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It is דינא, because the משנה, as explained, makes the robber who pointed out the field liable.

steps.title: רב יוסף asks why the difference matters
steps.stepSummary: After רב נחמן leaves, רב יוסף asks רב הונא בר חייא what practical difference there is between law and fine.
steps.simpleTranslation: After he left, רב יוסף said to רב הונא בר חייא: What difference does it make to you...
steps.whatsHappening: Once רב נחמן has left, רב יוסף turns to רב הונא בר חייא and asks why he cared whether it was law or a fine. The גמרא is setting up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Either way the man pays, so רב יוסף wants to know what practical result depends on the answer. This opens a new discussion about the real-life difference between דינא and קנסא.

keyTerms.meaning: a practical difference that comes out of it

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not finished here; it continues on the next amud.

phrases.english: After he left,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב יוֹסֵף לְרַב הוּנָא בַּר חִיָּיא:
phrases.english: Rav Yosef said to Rav Huna bar Chiyya:
What difference does it make to you

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the purpose of רב הונא בר חייא's question in Step 26.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What practical difference there is between the payment being דינא or קנסא.
